name: The Napoleon Oak
age_estimate: roughly 245-250 years, dated by dendrochronology to a germination around 1778

location.address: UNIL Dorigny campus, University of Lausanne

access: Free. Stands on the open, publicly accessible campus of the University of Lausanne (UNIL) at Dorigny.
transport: Lausanne metro (M1) to UNIL-Dorigny or UNIL-Sorge station, on the western edge of the city.
story:
Legend says this oak was planted for Napoleon. Its own wood says it was already here. In 2017 researchers dated its germination to around 1778 using tree-ring and genomic analysis, which makes it roughly 22 years old on 12 May 1800, the day Bonaparte reviewed 40,000 troops at Saint-Sulpice a few kilometres along the lake.

The local account, which nobody has withdrawn, is that Etienne-Francois-Louis de Loys, who then owned the Dorigny estate, planted the tree that year to mark the occasion. By that tradition it arrived as a transplanted sapling already two decades old and about 15 centimetres thick, which is not impossible and is not what most people picture when they hear that a tree was planted for Napoleon. The two versions sit side by side and we are leaving them there.

Either way it germinated before the French Revolution and it is still growing. French Wikipedia records 35 metres of height and 6.75 metres of circumference; some of the 2017 press coverage rounds those to 30 metres and about 7, and nobody has reconciled the figures.

What you cannot miss is the hardware. Roughly 140 metres of support cable now run through the crown to hold the limbs against their own weight. The oak stands on the open campus of the University of Lausanne, which has made it something of an emblem, and the metro puts you within a few minutes' walk.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the support cabling, roughly 140 metres of it strung through the crown, over a trunk 6.75 metres round and 35 metres of height. It stands on the open UNIL campus at Dorigny.
why_go: A 250-year-old oak on a university campus, wrapped in 140 metres of support cable to keep it standing, whose DNA was sequenced in 2017 to settle a local legend that it commemorates a visit from Napoleon himself.

name: The Giant Sequoia of Parc de Mon Repos

location.address: Parc de Mon Repos, near the amphitheatre

access: Free. Public historic park in central Lausanne.
transport: Central Lausanne, a short walk from Lausanne-Gare (main train station).
story:
This sequoia was already worth writing about in 1912, when Henri Badoux catalogued the notable trees of the canton and put it in the book. It has had another century of growing since. Lausanne now records it at 34 metres tall and 7.2 metres round, roughly 160 years old, which places its planting in the decades when European estates were competing to raise the newly imported giant sequoia and nobody had any idea what the things would do in Swiss soil.

It grows near the top of the amphitheatre in Parc de Mon Repos, with a ginkgo for a neighbour. The estate was where Pierre de Coubertin settled in 1922, some years after founding the modern Olympic movement, and the park is a short walk from the main station, which makes this an unusually easy giant tree to go and stand under.

The city classifies it as a remarkable tree and a local nature foundation calls it the finest giant sequoia in Lausanne, though all the measurements trace back to the municipal record rather than to two independent tapes.

Every giant sequoia in Europe is a beginner. The species reached the continent in the 1850s, so the oldest of them are still under two centuries, while the ones left standing in the Sierra Nevada run past two thousand years. This one has most of its life ahead of it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the thick spongy red bark of a giant sequoia and a trunk 7.2 metres round going 34 metres straight up. It stands near the top of the amphitheatre in Parc de Mon Repos, beside a ginkgo.
why_go: A 34-metre giant sequoia in the park where Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Olympics, made his home in 1922, officially recognised by the city as one of its remarkable trees.

name: The Weeping Beech of l'Hermitage
access: Free. Public historic park (Fondation de l'Hermitage art museum grounds are separately ticketed, but the park itself is open).
transport: Central Lausanne, uphill from the lakefront, roughly 15-20 minutes' walk from the train station or reachable by bus.
story:
The trunk this tree started with broke on the night of 20 June 2021, in a storm. The tree did not die, because it had spent the previous 170 years quietly planting itself. A weeping beech lets its branches fall to the ground, and where they touch and stay, they root. Long before the storm arrived, the original had raised a ring of daughter stems out of its own drooping limbs, genetically the same individual, and the City of Lausanne's record says plainly that these perpetuate its existence today.

So what stands at the top of Parc de l'Hermitage is less a specimen than a room. Old weeping beeches make a living cave: a curtain of branches down to the floor, a dim hollow inside, and generations of children who work out that you can walk into it. This one went in around 1851 and grew to 4.4 metres round, the landmark at the summit of the park.

One source carries all of that, the city's own tree-heritage page, and it is worth saying that we have found no second account and no recent photograph showing how the daughter growth is doing. If you climb up there, we would like to hear what you found.

The park itself is free. The art museum in the house beside it charges.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the shape, a weeping beech's curtain of branches down to the ground, now a ring of daughter stems grown from limbs that rooted where they touched. It stands at the summit of Parc de l'Hermitage.

best_time.label: May, when the new leaves close the curtain and the inside becomes a green room

why_go: Not a single trunk but a tree that turned into a grove: for 170 years its drooping branches rooted wherever they touched the ground, and when the original trunk finally broke in a 2021 storm, those rooted daughter stems, genetically the same individual, kept the tree alive on the same spot.
